This is the pastoral heart exposed: not the administrator worried about institutional health, but the father who grieves over his children.

13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The final chapter of 2 Corinthians brings the letter to its conclusion with a series of warnings, an extraordinary call to self-examination, and the most famous benediction in the New Testament. Paul announces his coming third visit: “This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.” He will not spare those who have sinned and not repented. He is not weak toward them: Christ is not weak in dealing with them but is powerful among them. The one crucified in weakness was raised in the power of God; Paul, who shares the weakness, also shares the power.

The call to self-examination (vv. 5–6) turns the tables on the Corinthians: they have been examining Paul, demanding proof that Christ speaks in him. Paul says: examine yourselves — test whether you are in the faith. This is not an invitation to doubt but a call to genuine self-knowledge. The Corinthians who know Christ is in them will recognise that Paul too is not disqualified. And Paul's ultimate desire is not that they recognise his authority but that they do what is right — even if it appears to disqualify him: “We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.”

The letter ends with the Trinitarian benediction of v. 14 — “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” — the most explicitly Trinitarian formula in the Pauline letters, placing all three persons in coordinate relation and ascribing to each a distinctive gift: grace (Christ), love (God the Father), fellowship (the Holy Spirit).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's announcement of his coming third visit carries the legal weight of Deuteronomy 19:15: every charge must be established by two or three witnesses. He has given a warning when present the second time; he is giving it again in writing now; when he comes, he will act. He is not weak toward them. The contrast with Christ is important: Christ was crucified in weakness but raised in power; Paul likewise, who shares Christ's weakness in his suffering, will also display the power of God when necessary. The weakness and the authority are both real and both derive from union with Christ.

The call to self-examination (vv. 5–6) is the most important pastoral move in the chapter. Rather than spending more time demanding that the Corinthians recognise his credentials, Paul redirects: examine yourselves. Test whether you are in the faith — ei este en tē pistei. The test he suggests: do you recognise that Christ is in you? If Christ is in you, then you can recognise the evidence of Christ in Paul. The sceptical Corinthians who demand proof of Paul's apostleship are being asked to first certify their own standing before God.
verseByVerse.theology: The call to self-examination (v. 5) has been used in Reformed tradition as the basis for the practice of self-examination before the Lord's Supper (1 Cor. 11:28–31). Genuine self-examination is not the cultivation of paralyzing doubt but the honest assessment of the soul before God: am I in the faith? Is Christ in me? Is my trust in Christ or in my own religious performance? The examination that produces assurance is the examination that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the examination that finds sufficient personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prepares for a communion service and the pastor leads a five-minute self-examination period before the elements are distributed. Some members treat it as a routine; others spiral into anxiety. This passage clarifies the goal: not to find sufficient personal holiness to “qualify” for the table, but to find whether Christ is there — whether the faith that receives him is genuine. The person who comes to the table trusting Christ is examining themselves correctly; the person who comes evaluating their performance has missed the point of both the examination and the table.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? — unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peirazete heautous (examine/test yourselves) — the verb peirazō means to test with a view to proving, often used for testing metals for purity. The self-examination is not navel-gazing but quality assurance: is what I believe genuine faith, or is it religious habit, cultural Christianity, or self-deception? The criterion is not the absence of doubt or the presence of strong religious feeling but the recognition that “Jesus Christ is in you” — the indwelling Christ as the ground of assurance.

“We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth” (v. 8) — one of Paul's most striking statements about the ultimate invincibility of the gospel. Paul's authority, his ministry, his entire apostolic enterprise is in the service of the truth; it cannot be wielded against it. This is the principle of ministerial accountability: the minister's authority is derived from and limited by the truth of the gospel. Any exercise of authority that contradicts the gospel is not legitimate authority but its perversion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul closes with a rapid series of imperatives: rejoice, aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace — and the promise: the God of love and peace will be with you. The holy kiss and greetings from the saints of Macedonia complete the personal frame.

The final benediction (v. 14) is the most explicitly Trinitarian formula in the Pauline letters: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” Each person of the Trinity is named; each is given a distinctive gift. Grace (charis) is attributed to the Lord Jesus Christ — the undeserved favour that flows from his person and work. Love (agapē) is attributed to God the Father — the initiating, originating love that sent the Son (John 3:16; Rom. 5:8). Fellowship (koinōnia) is attributed to the Holy Spirit — the participation in the divine life, the communion with God and one another, that the Spirit creates and sustains.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction is not a formula but a theology: it presents the three persons in distinct but coordinated action, each contributing uniquely to the believer's life. The order (Christ, Father, Spirit) is unusual — the more common Pauline order puts the Father first — possibly because the letter's concerns have centred on the grace of Christ (the atonement of ch. 5, the self-giving of ch. 8). The coordinated action of all three persons in the single benediction is an implicit trinitarian claim: to receive grace, love, and fellowship from these three distinct persons is to receive from one God in three persons.

Koinōnia of the Holy Spirit — three possible meanings, all theologically valid: (1) the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers; (2) participation in the Spirit — sharing in the Spirit's life; (3) the Spirit as the one who communicates fellowship with the Father and Son. These are not mutually exclusive; the Spirit's work achieves all three simultaneously. Those who are indwelt by the Spirit share in the divine koinōnia — the mutual love and life of the Trinity — and that sharing is expressed in genuine community with one another.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that closes every service with this benediction has been pronouncing it for decades as a familiar liturgical ending. A new pastor stops before pronouncing it and asks the congregation: do you know what you are about to receive? Each phrase is unpacked slowly — the grace that flows from Christ's cross, the love that originated in the Father's heart before creation, the fellowship that the Spirit creates both with God and among the gathered community. The familiar words suddenly land with the weight they have always carried. The benediction is not a farewell; it is a sending into the world with the fullness of the Triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The benediction formula is unique in Paul — no other letter has exactly this form, though the components appear throughout his writings (grace of Christ: Rom. 16:20; Gal. 6:18; Phil. 4:23; love of God: Rom. 8:39; fellowship of the Spirit: Phil. 2:1). The explicit coordination of all three persons in a single benedictive statement is the NT's clearest pre-Nicene articulation of what will become trinitarian doctrine.

“Be with you all” (meta pantōn hymōn) — the benediction is inclusive, even of those who have been resistant and challenging throughout the letter. Paul does not conclude with a blessing for the faithful and a warning for the recalcitrant; he extends the grace, love, and fellowship of the Triune God to the whole community. The Trinity does not play favourites; the grace that is sufficient for Paul's weakness is offered to the whole Corinthian church in all its messiness and division.
